title: The daughter who argued
hook: Princess Ruja rescues her father from a false teaching (Jataka 544)

segments.voice: Yesterday: uposatha, the observance day, and a naga prince who kept his precepts in a snake charmer's basket. Your line: he kept it. Today, a princess who won't let her father's mistake stand.

On a bright festival night, King Angati of Mithila asks his advisers what would make the evening complete. One suggests visiting a famous ascetic. The ascetic, Guna, tells the king something that sounds like freedom: there is no fruit of deeds. Good or bad, nothing you do comes back. What will be, will be. The king goes home convinced. Today, the person who argues him out of it: his daughter.
screen: `A FESTIVAL NIGHT.` → `NO FRUIT OF DEEDS.` → `THE KING IS CONVINCED.`

segments.voice: Angati stops giving. He closes his gifts to the poor and turns to his own pleasures, since nothing, he now believes, makes a difference. Then Princess Ruja comes to him, as she regularly does, to ask for money for her own gifts. He refuses and explains his new view. And she argues. Respectfully, calling him father, but she doesn't back down. The story says she could remember past lives, and she tells him of one where a wrong she did came back to her in suffering. Deeds have fruit, she says; she has seen it. The king won't move. So Ruja turns to the directions and asks, in effect, for any good being in the world to come and help. Narada, a being from a high heaven, comes down dressed as an ascetic, and with patience and vivid pictures of where deeds lead, brings the king back to giving and to his precepts. Tradition pairs this tale with equanimity, upekkha. The one who stands up to the false teaching isn't a sage or a minister. It's a daughter, speaking up at home, to her own father, with no guarantee he'll listen. She argues with love, not contempt, and she asks for help when her own words run out. That's the shape of disagreeing well.
screen: `THE KING STOPS GIVING.` · `RUJA ARGUES, RESPECTFULLY.` · `SHE ASKS FOR HELP.` · `NARADA BRINGS HIM BACK.` · then, large: `THE DAUGHTER ARGUED.`

segments.voice: Choose a small belief you've taken as settled, like nothing changes anyway, or they'll never listen, and hold it up to the light: what have you actually seen? Don't attack it or defend it; just ask, the way Ruja asked her father, with respect and without backing down.
Ruja. The king's daughter who argued against his belief that deeds have no fruit, and asked the heavens for help when her own words ran out.
Your line: the daughter argued. Respect and disagreement can share one voice. That's day eight hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Buddhist teaching holds that intentional actions, kamma, bear fruit; the tale of Ruja and Narada is told to show why that teaching matters for how a person lives and gives.

chat.says: Did Princess Ruja change her father's mind all by herself?
options: No. She argued with respect, and when he wouldn't move, she asked for help.
Yes. One clever speech about her past lives convinced him at once.
No. She gave up arguing and left the palace in protest.
chat.meaning: The king wouldn't move for Ruja alone. She called on any good being to help, and Narada came and brought him back.

Guna.meaning: the ascetic who taught that deeds bear no fruit

Ruja.meaning: the princess who argued with her father

Narada.meaning: a being from a high heaven who came to help

upekkha.meaning: equanimity, an even and balanced mind

notes: The index says Ruja 'rescues her father'; the script keeps her central but follows the Jataka: she argues, cannot convince him alone, and appeals for help, and Narada (the Bodhisatta, a Brahma) brings the king back. Keeper to confirm this reading of the index line.

Confirm: the full-moon festival night; Guna Kassapa's view that deeds bear no fruit; the king's turn from giving; Ruja's request for money for alms; her memory of past lives (the text gives a number of lives, omitted here) and a past life of suffering for wrongdoing; her homage to the directions; Narada's descent in ascetic's guise.
Guna's view is presented only as the story's false teaching, not linked to any present-day school; confirm.
Confirm the traditional pairing Narada = upekkha (equanimity).
